title: The Tragedy of the Accelerator
author: The Bootleg Manager
summary: Told as a five-act Shakespearean tragedy, this piece recounts the author's early-career experience leading 'The Accelerator,' a marketing technology platform commissioned by a director who had already signed a vendor contract before any needs analysis was done. As the newly hired project lead, the author discovers that colleagues' workflows differ legitimately by product team, that no one is actually reading the reports the new system is meant to improve, and that a cheaper off-the-shelf tool would have met the stated goals -- but is overruled because the contract is already signed. The narrative tracks the project's slow collapse: mounting customization costs, colleague disengagement, and the author's dawning recognition of the sunk cost fallacy, all while deferring to the director's authority because, as the piece puts it, if the leader is certain you should be too. The project is ultimately killed by a successor leader after the original director leaves for another job. The essay's larger argument is that 'because the boss said so' is not a business case, and that secondhand certainty collapses as soon as real scrutiny arrives.
points: The author's early instinct to investigate before building revealed the actual problem didn't exist as described: colleagues' varied processes reflected different product teams' genuine needs, and no one on the receiving end was reading the existing reports.
An off-the-shelf competitor tool that could have met the stated goals was rejected outright because the team was already committed to a contract signed before any requirements analysis took place.

The build repeatedly hit the sunk cost fallacy: every new limitation surfaced by developers was resolved by 'another training issue' or by spending more of the budget, never by questioning the original premise.

The essay's central diagnostic questions for evaluating any leader-driven initiative: What do we do now? Who suffers from the current way of doing things? Would the proposed solution actually solve it?
The project was killed within weeks of a leadership change, illustrating how much organizational effort can be sustained purely by deference to authority rather than evidence.
quotes: My colleagues all did things differently - because each served a different product team, with different goals and different needs. Each product team set its own priorities, which drove my colleagues' decision-making.

How hard would it be, I wondered aloud, to cancel the contract for the vendor he'd chosen? It would be so much easier to just use this existing platform, as-is, instead of trying to mold an unrelated system to our needs.

I was starting to fully understand the term I'd learned in grad school: sunk cost fallacy. We'd already put so much time, effort, and money into The Aggravator - but did what we'd already spent justify spending even more?

If the leader is certain, you should be certain, too. Or at least willing to suspend your own doubts in favor of what that leader deems to be true. As I learned the hard way, secondhand certainty only goes so far.
A new leader was swiftly appointed. He took stock of what our team was doing and made some changes. He didn't slow down the Accelerator project - he killed it.
But if someone had point-blank asked me why we needed this platform, my only true answer would have been, "Because Dave said so.
